vignette:
Amina is a 73-year-old African American woman who has spent most of her adult life in the Army and now presents for help after surviving a natural disaster that shook the structure of her days and her sense of safety. She is single, still identifies herself first as a soldier, and speaks in the disciplined, sparing way of someone used to enduring hardship without asking much from anyone else. The disaster itself remains the central fact of her story. She describes being on base during a violent storm that escalated with little warning, the air changing first, then the sound of metal straining and alarms carrying across the compound. She remembers water pushing into buildings, equipment shifting, people shouting over each other, and the strange helplessness of seeing a familiar military environment become suddenly ungovernable. What stands out in the way she tells it is not embellishment but the starkness: the noise, the force of the weather, the moment she understood that training and rank did not place anyone outside danger.

In the weeks after, Amina did not think of herself as having a psychological problem. She thought of herself as having survived and needing to continue. She kept reporting for duty, maintaining her routines as best she could, and speaking about the event in practical terms. At her age, and after a lifetime in uniform, she is uncomfortable with language that sounds like vulnerability. She says she has seen many things and managed many crises, and part of her distress now lies in the contrast between that self-image and the fact that this event has stayed with her in a way she did not expect. She is embarrassed by needing support and has delayed seeking care longer than she likely would have advised someone under her command to delay.

Her work setting remains the place where the disaster feels most immediate. Military installations are organized around preparedness, drills, weather alerts, heavy equipment, and rapid shifts in atmosphere, and for Amina those ordinary features now carry a different emotional charge. She notices how often the environment places her back in contact with reminders of what happened: the metallic echo in large structures, the public address system, the sight of storm barriers and emergency vehicles staged near buildings. Even when she tries to stay focused on tasks, she finds that the base itself no longer feels simply familiar. It is the same physical setting in which she once felt competent and anchored, and that contrast is painful for her to sit with.

Over time, the strain of carrying this on her own has become harder to deny. She has become more inward, less inclined to linger in conversation, and more likely to keep her experience to a few clipped sentences before shutting it down. Being single has meant there is no one at home who automatically sees the toll the disaster has taken, and she has become practiced at presenting a composed exterior. Colleagues see an older soldier who still comes in and gets things done; they do not necessarily see the effort behind that steadiness. In session, she gives the impression of someone who has spent months trying to outlast her distress through sheer discipline.

What finally brought her in was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of too many moments in which the disaster no longer felt fully in the past. She began to recognize that she was organizing more of her life around getting through the day than actually living it. That realization unsettled her. She had always believed that if she kept moving, kept working, and held herself to the standards she had lived by for decades, the impact of the storm would recede on its own. Instead, she found herself increasingly aware that the event still occupied a central place in her mind and in the way she moved through her environment.

At intake, Amina is controlled, dignified, and wary of being seen as weak, but also tired of carrying this alone. What she wants most is not sympathy; it is to feel steady again in a world that no longer feels reliably secure. What frightens her is the possibility that this experience has changed her permanently, that after a lifetime of being the person others could count on, she may no longer be able to rely on herself in the same way. She is seeking help now with a quiet, reluctant hope that putting words to what happened might allow the disaster to become something she survived rather than something she is still living inside.
